Fate is tricky, I started out with Fate/Zero and I have had a ton of fun with the Fate series as a whole. I do recognize some big reveals were ruined for me, but I don't really mind that much. The different routes in the visual novel were forced as Fate > UBW > HF, and this is for a reason. Each route has the main character growing from one ideological standpoint to another, so if you were to view the series as intended you should start with the original. But the animation is so bad compared to what we have now, you might as well watch that first so you can get through it or read the visual novel. Ufotable's animation will spoil you.

GITS is a classic and a favorite of mine, I think it's worth watching so you can see its influence on other titles (particularly The Matrix).

Kara no Kyoukai's movies are all connected in some way, and the first and last are directly connected. They can be confusing, you need to trust the movies to provide you the explanations eventually. The first 4 movies are also out of order. (Some people find that to be a spoiler but I think it's better to know to hold on to your sanity.) The fact that they're movies means that the story flow is different, meaning that the "Rising Action" and "Climax" etc are set up differently than how it would be if it were 30 minute episodes.

In term of technical stuff, the animation is amazing (usual Ufotable fare) and the soundtrack is widely regarded as Yuki Kaijura's best.

Fissionism: Why Libertarianism Should Extricate Itself from Conservative Entanglements

I couldn't agree more. I'm extremely liberal in my attitudes and a hardcore minarchist. I think there are plenty of others like me that are turned off libertarianism because it's so muddled with conservatism.

I'm about as socially liberal as possible (I live in Portland and am friends with just about every stereotype we've got); wouldn't mind a basic minimum income or negative income tax as only government service beyond police, military, and courts; and more.

I think there are tons of people like me who don't mind a social safety net and a few services like roads, but want the government out of everything else (like markets, bedrooms, etc.). Libertarians are a lot closer to that than the Democrats, that's for sure.

As a former left-liberal who thinks both Roads and wages are able to be provided by market forces I whole heartedly agree.

Further reading: https://mises.org/library/privatization-roads-and-highways

https://mises.org/sites/default/files/Man,%20Economy,%20and%20State,%20with%20Power%20and%20Market_2.pdf especially chapter 8, entrepreneurship and change

"That the general trend of original-factor incomes and prices may well be downward is a startling conclusion, for it is difficult to conceive of a progressing economy as one in which factor prices, such as wage rates and ground rents, steadily decline.

What interests us, however, is not the course of money incomes and prices of factors, but of real incomes and prices, i.e., the “goods-income” accruing to factors. If money wage rates or wage incomes fall, and the supply of consumers’ goods increases such that the prices of these goods fall even more, the result is a rise in “real” wage rates and “real incomes” to factors. That this is precisely what does happen solves the paradox that a progressing economy experiences falling wages and rents. There may be a fall in money terms (although not in all conceivable cases); but there will always be a rise in real terms.

The rise in real rates and incomes is due to the increase in the marginal physical productivity of factors that always results from an increase in saving and investment.10 The increased productivity of the longer production processes leads to a greater physical supply of capital goods, and, most important, of consumers’ goods, with a consequent fall in the prices of consumers’ goods.

As a result, even if the money prices of labor and land fall, those of consumers’ goods will always fall farther, so that real factor incomes will rise. "

I take the opposite view. Because our views are so well defined it's easy to identify every way in which a proposal deviates from our ideals. We can see exactly how anyone has "sold out" or settled for anything less than perfection. This tends to make us dogmatic and unyielding, incapable of forming coalitions with people we only agree with partially or to make the compromises necessary to win partial victories. But partial victories, compromise with people we only agree with in part to achieve gradual progress are the only path to success in a democracy. Nobody ever "wins" a complete victory in a democracy because nobody entirely agrees with anyone else. The best you can ever hope for is to get part of what you want today as a foundation to work for more tomorrow and you have to work with people that want something different because you need to get to 50%+1 and you only have 10% or less that really truly agree with you.

Conservatism is always going to be influential in any nation's politics. In the case of the USA libertarianism has had a huge influence on conservatism in america to the degree that libertarian ideas are most often misidentified as "conservative" in the public mind, and by most conservatives themselves. This is partly because there are a lot of classically liberal aspects to our political traditions and the "reformers" who want to change things (and change is what conservatives really oppose) are seeking to make things less liberal. In those cases conservatives and classical liberals are natural allies if only from expediency.

But we've also influenced american conservatives because of Fusionism. Fusionism has led conservatives generally to adopt libertarian rhetoric and many have come to believe in them at least partially, and despite being notoriously inconsistent. That libertarian strain within the much larger and more influential conservative movement has been growing in size and influence. It'd be shortsighted and self-destructive to abandon a successful coalition which has been continually (if slowly) moving our way in a fit of idealistic disillusionment.

Imagine we create special subverses and alt accounts to post in them (tied to a sub, with a tag for example). To ensure that it stays a game and doesn't annoy real subverses.

Upvoating and Downvoating are now weapons.You can help your friends by giving them upvoats, thus granting them the possibility to upvoat more each day or even to downvoat (the holy Grail). By downvoating enemies you rob them of their daily upvoats and could even stop them from downvoating your allies. An enemy who cannot upvoat because his/her CCP is negative is as good as dead --until friends come to the rescue.

As I see it, each sub would have a stickied thread in which all users who want to play would post only one comment. Enemies would target users in this thread only.The thread would need to be recreated each week, for example, to know who is still or isn't an active player.

Brigading is an assault, a battle, in a war. Winners would emerge as subs with the most power. Enough power to significantly hinder other's upvoat and downvoat capabilities, but also to be brigaded and recover quickly.
